top_topics.topic: Aerodynamics and Acoustics in Jet Flows

top_cited_works.title: Structure of the Compressible Turbulent Shear Layer
top_cited_works.abstract: The large-scale structure of the turbulent compressible shear layer is investigated in a two-stream supersonic wind tunnel. Double-exposure schlieren photography reveals that the two convective Mach numbers, corresponding to each side of the shear layer, are very different: one is sonic or supersonic and the other is low subsonic. This contradicts the current isentropic large-scale-structure model, which predicts the convective Mach numbers to be equal or very close. It is speculated that effects of shock waves are responsible for these asymmetries.

top_cited_works.title: The compressible turbulent shear layer: an experimental study
top_cited_works.abstract: The growth rate and turbulent structure of the compressible, plane shear layer are investigated experimentally in a novel facility. In this facility, it is possible to flow similar or dissimilar gases of different densities and to select different Mach numbers for each stream. Ten combinations of gases and Mach numbers are studied in which the free-stream Mach numbers range from 0.2 to 4. Schlieren photography of 20-ns exposure time reveals very low spreading rates and large-scale structures. The growth of the turbulent region is defined by means of Pitot-pressure profiles measured at several streamwise locations. A compressibility-effect parameter is defined that correlates and unifies the experimental results. It is the Mach number in a coordinate system convecting with the velocity of the dominant waves and structures of the shear layer, called here the convective Mach number. It happens to have nearly the same value for each stream. In the current experiments, it ranges from 0 to 1.9. top_cited_works.title: Observations of supersonic free shear layers
top_cited_works.abstract: Visual spreading rates of turbulent shear layers with at least one stream supersonic were measured using Schlieren photography. The experiments were done at a variety of Mach number-gas combinations. The spreading rates are correlated with a compressibility-effect parameter called the convective Mach number. It is found that for supersonic values of the convective Mach number, the spreading rate is about one quarter that of an incompressible layer at the same velocity and density ratio. The results are compared with other experimental and theoretical results.

recent_works.title: Noise Suppression from High-Speed Jet Using Localized Secondary Parallel Injection
recent_works.abstract: This paper presents an experimental parametric study of noise reduction from a high-speed jet using localized, parallel injection of secondary air. The intent is suppression of noise in directions relevant to deck crew exposure during operation of tactical aircraft from aircraft carriers. The secondary stream is operated at a lower speed than the primary jet, reducing the ability of the primary turbulent eddies to emit strong Mach waves. The experiments are performed under conditions realistic to high-performance turbofan engines, with a primary exhaust speed of 870 m/s and a mass flow rate ratio of 0.28 for the secondary injection. The effects of injector exhaust shape, azimuthal aperture, and azimuthal orientation are investigated. A simple factorial design is based on an acoustic figure of merit that considers the sound power level over a sector relevant to crew exposure. recent_works.title: Wind Tunnel Continuous-Scan Acoustic Analysis of Ducted Fan Tones Interacting With a Shielding Wall
recent_works.abstract: Abstract High-bypass ratio ducted fans emit tonal and broadband noise in both forward and aft directions. While produced by common mechanisms, the noise radiating in each direction is typically treated as its own directional source. Proper modeling of forward- and aft-emitted fan noise enables more efficient noise suppression strategies. In this article, wind tunnel continuous-scan (CS) acoustic measurements of a fan simulator are analyzed in two configurations: with and without a barrier wall structure. The barrier wall is used to separate the forward-emitted fan noise from the aft-emitted fan noise through shielding. As acoustic shielding is also an important noise reduction strategy for next-generation aircraft, the barrier wall is an effective surrogate to study the effect of propulsion airframe aeroacoustics (PAA), where the wall creates shielding and/or scattering similar to a wing or airframe surface. recent_works.title: Elements of aeroacoustics of high-speed turbulence
Acoustic Simulation of a High-Speed Jet with Localized Parallel Injection of Secondary Flow
recent_works.abstract: Wall-Modeled Large Eddy Simulation (WMLES) of a high-speed jet with localized, parallel injection of secondary air is investigated. The injection scheme is designed to attenuate turbofan exhaust noise affecting launch crew personnel on an aircraft carrier deck. The focus of the computation is on understanding and eventually modeling the physical mechanisms of noise reduction measured experimentally. The simulated geometry is selected from previous experimental studies that yielded a 5.2 dBA reduction in the peak overall sound pressure level (OASPL) in the far field, in directions relevant to crew exposure. Analysis of the simulation data encompasses traditional statistics, axial space-time correlations that yielded convective velocities, spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD), and propagation to the far field using a Ffowcs-Williams and Hawkings surface.
